strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful question: distributional symmetry and target-function equivariance are distinct, and their interaction matters when choosing augmentation or equivariant architectures.

The classifier diagnostic is simple and broadly applicable. Experiments cover several scientific and vision datasets, with synthetic rotation controls, architecture-size ablations, MMD comparisons, and informative local-versus-global analyses.

The under-parameterized regression analysis usefully distinguishes training augmentation from test-time symmetrization. Extensive appendices provide derivations, simulation details, and experimental configurations.
weaknesses: Theorem 3(ii) contains an infeasible condition. Since dc < d0, the limiting ratios satisfy gamma_c <= gamma_0. For gamma_c > 1, this implies gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 >= gamma_c/2 > 1/2, contradicting the required inequality gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 < 1/2. The appendix repeats this condition, and the simulations cover only gamma_c < 1. Consequently, the claimed harmful-augmentation regime in part (ii) is vacuous as stated. Its bias expression also omits the sigma_c factor present in Appendix Eq. (56).

The methodological novelty is limited: the main diagnostic directly applies an established classifier two-sample test to the original and group-averaged distributions. Related work already considers both discriminative symmetry discovery and comparison with group-averaged distributions. The paper does not establish a substantial methodological advantage over these approaches.

The interpretation of classifier accuracy overreaches the evidence. Optimal balanced accuracy equals (1 + TV(p, p_bar))/2, but a trained classifier generally provides only a lower bound on this optimum. Low accuracy can therefore reflect insufficient classifier power rather than approximate symmetry. Architecture-size ablations on highly separable QM9 do not resolve this issue for local neighborhoods or harder distributions; Appendix B itself demonstrates such a failure on Swiss Roll.

The main empirical narrative about QM9 is inconsistent with the complete results. Section 5 says augmentation helps nearly all properties, but Table 5 shows train-only augmentation worsening alpha, R2, ZPVE, U0, U, and H relative to no augmentation—six of twelve targets. Table 1 presents a favorable subset. This materially weakens the claimed contrast between molecular datasets and MNIST/ModelNet40.

Evaluation reliability is insufficient for several conclusions. Appendix C.4.1 explicitly reports minimum test MAE across training, rather than results from validation-selected checkpoints. The main downstream comparisons lack repeated-run uncertainty, despite some differences being very small. ModelNet40 results also use a nonstandard split and relatively weak models, leaving the generality of the observed augmentation penalties uncertain.

The diagnostic is not convincingly connected to the decision posed in the title. High scores occur with both beneficial and harmful augmentation, the per-class ModelNet40 analysis finds no relationship with augmentation gains, and the task-dependent extension is architecture-sensitive and inconclusive on realistic datasets. The locality explanation remains observational and does not establish that local symmetry causes the benefits. These limitations, together with the theoretical and evaluation issues, place the paper below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant distinction between invariant target functions and invariant input distributions, highlighting why symmetry assumptions deserve scrutiny.

The empirical investigation is broad, covering images, point clouds, molecular datasets, and crystal representations. Synthetic augmentation controls, architecture ablations, and appendix comparisons with MMD strengthen the evidence for detectable distributional asymmetry.
The separation of training augmentation from test-time symmetrization is useful. The underparameterized analysis and simulations provide concrete examples of their different statistical behavior.
The appendix provides substantial experimental details, and the paper openly acknowledges that its task-dependent metric is inconclusive on several datasets.
weaknesses: Theorem 3(ii) contains an impossible condition. The assumptions imply gamma_c <= gamma_0, so gamma_c > 1 implies gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 >= gamma_c/2 > 1/2, contradicting the required inequality gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 < 1/2. Consequently, this claimed regime of harmful augmentation is empty. The theorem also omits the sigma_c factor present in its corresponding bias expression, Equation (56). These issues require correction and reassessment of the theoretical conclusions.

The methodological novelty is limited: the main diagnostic applies an established classifier two-sample test to original versus group-augmented data. Related symmetry-discovery and invariance-testing approaches already address closely related questions. The appendix comparisons are useful but do not establish a compelling advantage in statistical power, sample efficiency, or computational cost.

Classifier accuracy is not an architecture-independent measure of distributional asymmetry. Optimal balanced accuracy equals (1 + TV(p, p_bar))/2, whereas a trained classifier can substantially underestimate it. The Swiss-roll example explicitly demonstrates this limitation. Robustness to transformer size on QM9 does not establish reliable comparisons across datasets or between local and global representations.

The connection to deciding whether augmentation helps remains unresolved. High diagnostic scores accompany both beneficial and harmful augmentation; Appendix C.1.2 finds no clear relationship with the augmentation benefit across ModelNet40 classes; and the task-dependent extension is architecture-sensitive. The locality experiments suggest a hypothesis but do not establish that locality explains the downstream performance differences.

The downstream evaluation has important reliability limitations. Table 1 lacks uncertainty across training runs, and Appendix C.4.1 explicitly reports minimum test MAEs rather than clearly documenting validation-selected checkpoints. Some reported improvements are small enough that these omissions matter. The relatively weak custom baselines and limited tuning evidence also restrict conclusions about equivariant methods generally.

The QM9 narrative overstates the consistency of augmentation benefits. In Table 5, train-only augmentation improves over no augmentation on only six of twelve properties, worsening alpha, R2, ZPVE, U0, U, and H. The main table emphasizes favorable properties, while the conclusion states that augmentation only impedes performance on MNIST and ModelNet40.

The strongest negative theoretical results concern Gaussian linear regression in ridgeless asymptotic regimes with specially structured covariance. Although informative as counterexamples, they do not establish persistence under appropriately tuned regularization or explain the neural-network experiments. This gap, together with the theorem error and evaluation limitations, leaves the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important distinction between symmetry of the target function and symmetry of the input distribution, with practical relevance to augmentation and equivariant learning.
The classifier diagnostic is simple and interpretable. Experiments cover diverse datasets, include controlled augmentation checks, and investigate both global and local symmetry breaking.

The under-parameterized analysis usefully distinguishes training augmentation from test-time symmetrization. The strong-correlation example and simulations demonstrate that augmentation can hurt despite invariant labels.
The appendix provides extensive experimental details, architecture ablations, kernel-based comparisons, and candid discussion of inconclusive task-dependent results.
weaknesses: Theorem 3(ii) contains an infeasible condition. Since dc < d0 implies gamma_c <= gamma_0, gamma_c > 1 implies gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 >= gamma_c/2 > 1/2, contradicting the required inequality gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 < 1/2. Thus this claimed regime is empty. Appendix A.7.1 repeats the condition, while the simulations only examine gamma_c < 1 and cannot validate this branch.

Additional theoretical inconsistencies need correction: Theorem 2 omits the signal-norm factor in its bias term without stating unit normalization; Theorem 3's bias omits sigma_c, which appears in Equation (56); and Equation (47)'s quadratic coefficient has the wrong sign on the (g - gamma_c)w term when derived from Equation (45). These undermine confidence in the over-parameterized analysis as presented.

The downstream evaluation is insufficiently reliable. Section C.4.1 explicitly reports minimum test MAE rather than performance at validation-selected checkpoints, introducing test-selection bias. Tables 1 and 5 lack uncertainty across repeated training runs, making small gains difficult to assess. The relatively weak ModelNet40 baselines and limited tuning evidence also restrict broader conclusions about equivariant methods.

The diagnostic's methodological novelty is limited: it applies an established classifier two-sample test to original versus symmetrized data. Optimal accuracy is simply (1 + TV(p, p_bar))/2; learned accuracy additionally depends on classifier capacity and optimization. The Swiss-roll example demonstrates that chance accuracy can occur for canonicalized data, so architecture-size robustness on QM9 does not establish a generally reliable quantitative measure.

The connection between measured asymmetry and augmentation utility remains unresolved. Highly asymmetric datasets show opposite augmentation outcomes, class-level ModelNet40 scores do not predict augmentation gains, and the task-dependent metric is inconclusive on realistic datasets. Locality experiments provide suggestive observations but no controlled intervention establishing the proposed explanation. Combined with the theoretical and evaluation issues, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance.

strengths: Addresses a relevant question: distributional symmetry need not follow from label equivariance, and enforcing invariance can affect in-distribution performance.
The classifier diagnostic is simple and interpretable. Synthetic augmentation experiments, architecture and sample-size ablations, and comparisons with MMD provide useful validation.

The empirical investigation spans several datasets and includes augmentation, equivariant architectures, group averaging, local neighborhoods, and task-dependent diagnostics. Reporting cases where augmentation remains beneficial despite strong asymmetry adds useful nuance.
The under-parameterized analysis clearly distinguishes training augmentation from test-time symmetrization. The appendix provides substantial experimental details and theoretical derivations.
weaknesses: Theorem 2(ii) contains an impossible condition under its stated assumptions. Since dc < d0 implies γc ≤ γ0 and this case assumes γc > 1, necessarily γ0 − γc/2 ≥ γc/2 > 1/2. Therefore, the condition γ0 − γc/2 < 1/2 cannot hold, making the claimed variance comparison vacuous. The theorem's bias expression also omits the σc factor present in Appendix equation (59). These issues require correction before the theoretical contribution can be relied upon.

Appendix C.2 incorrectly claims an affine equivalence between independently optimized dependence detection and label prediction. A binary dependence classifier can accept several labels for one orientation; selecting any accepted label does not preserve its discrimination advantage. For example, with four equally likely labels and an orientation identifying which pair contains the label, optimal m1 is 0.75 while optimal m2 is 0.25, contradicting m2 = 2m1 − 1.

The main diagnostic largely applies an established classifier two-sample test to an existing original-versus-symmetrized distribution comparison. Related discriminative symmetry-discovery methods are acknowledged, but the methodological advance is limited. The MMD experiments do not establish a compelling advantage in detection power, calibration, or computational cost.

The proposed augmentation recommendations are supported mainly by retrospective agreement on a small set of tasks. ModelNet40 is the principal natural example of substantial harm, while the dipole-aligned example deliberately constructs label-dependent orientation. There is no validated decision threshold or held-out-task evaluation showing that t(pX,Y) reliably selects augmentation strategies. Low classifier accuracy also cannot establish symmetry without controlling approximation and optimization error.

The downstream comparisons do not establish robustness across competitive architectures and tuning choices. ModelNet40 results are approximately 60–78% in the main table, and parameter-count matching alone does not isolate equivariance from architectural differences. The additional transformer experiment is helpful, but broader controlled comparisons and regularization sweeps are needed to connect the ridgeless theory to practical neural-network behavior.

The evaluation protocol raises a specific concern: Appendix D.4.1 states that minimum test MAEs are reported. If checkpoints were selected using test performance, the reported results are optimistically biased; validation-based selection and a final untouched test evaluation are needed. The local-neighborhood findings are also observational: lower detection accuracy does not establish that local isotropy causes the benefits of equivariance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: when distributional asymmetry changes the benefits of augmentation and equivariant models. It usefully distinguishes distributional symmetry breaking from non-equivariant target functions.

The empirical investigation is broad, covering molecular datasets, ModelNet40, MNIST, and crystal representations. Synthetic rotation controls, architecture and sample-size ablations, MMD comparisons, and repeated runs provide useful evidence that the classifier detects substantial distributional asymmetry.

The distinction between training augmentation and test-time symmetrization is valuable. The under-parameterized analysis and the simulated over-parameterized example provide concrete insight beyond simply reporting benchmark correlations.
weaknesses: Theorem 2(ii) contains an impossible condition. The construction requires dc < d0, hence gamma_c <= gamma_0 asymptotically. When gamma_c > 1, this implies gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 >= gamma_c/2 > 1/2, contradicting the stated condition gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 < 1/2. Consequently, this claimed regime of harmful augmentation is empty. The theorem also omits the sigma_c factor present in its appendix bias expression, equation (59). These issues materially weaken the theoretical contribution, although they do not invalidate the separate gamma_c < 1 example.

Appendix C.2 incorrectly claims an affine equivalence between optimized dependence detection and label prediction. Choosing any label accepted by a dependence classifier does not establish the reverse inequality: multiple labels can be positively associated with the same canonicalization. For example, with four equiprobable labels and a canonicalization identifying which pair contains the label, optimal m1 is 0.75 while optimal m2 is 0.25, contradicting m2 = 2m1 - 1. Furthermore, this analysis does not establish properties of the rotation-based loss ratio actually used in the main experiments.

The practical recommendations in Figure 6 exceed the evidence. Low classifier accuracy can reflect insufficient detection power rather than symmetry, as the paper's own Swiss-roll example demonstrates. Nevertheless, the flowchart recommends equivariant methods when m is near chance. The task-dependent metric is evaluated on relatively few tasks without a validated decision threshold or prospective test of its ability to predict augmentation benefits.

The evaluation does not adequately establish that the observed augmentation penalties persist under strong, appropriately tuned models. ModelNet40 results use a custom 80/10/10 split and relatively weak classifiers; the additional transformer experiment helps but does not resolve this concern. More seriously, Appendix D.4.1 explicitly reports minimum test MAEs over training for QM9, introducing test-set selection bias instead of selecting checkpoints by validation performance.

The primary diagnostic has limited methodological novelty: it applies an established classifier two-sample test to a distribution and its group average, closely related to prior symmetry-detection approaches acknowledged by the authors. Appendix D.10 includes useful MMD comparisons, but does not establish a compelling advantage in calibrated power, computational cost, or downstream decision quality.

The theory-to-practice connection remains incomplete. The harmful-augmentation result relies on a particular covariance model and the ridgeless limit; the paper does not establish whether the disadvantage survives separately tuned regularization. Likewise, lower detection accuracy on local fragments is suggestive but does not establish that local equivariance causes the molecular performance gains. These limitations, combined with the mathematical errors, leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: label equivariance does not imply symmetry of the input distribution. Distinguishing these assumptions is useful for understanding augmentation and equivariant architectures.

The classifier diagnostic is simple, interpretable, and broadly applicable. Experiments cover images, point clouds, molecular datasets, and atom permutations, with synthetic rotation controls, architecture and sample-size ablations, and MMD comparisons in the appendix.

The theoretical analysis usefully distinguishes training-time augmentation from test-time symmetrization. The under-parameterized result and the strongly correlated, over-parameterized example provide concrete mechanisms for different generalization behavior.

The empirical discussion acknowledges counterexamples to the initial intuition: molecular tasks often benefit from equivariance despite substantial distributional asymmetry. The task-dependent and local-neighborhood analyses offer interesting follow-up hypotheses.
weaknesses: Theorem 2(ii) contains a substantive inconsistency. The construction requires dc < d0, hence gamma_c <= gamma_0 asymptotically. With gamma_c > 1, this implies gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 >= gamma_c/2 > 1/2, so the stated condition gamma_0 - gamma_c/2 < 1/2 cannot hold. The corresponding variance claim is therefore vacuous. The theorem also omits the sigma_c factor present in the appendix's bias expression, Equation (59). These issues require correction before the theoretical contribution can be considered reliable.

The main diagnostic applies an established classifier two-sample test to the original and group-averaged distributions; both classifier tests and distributional symmetry testing have substantial prior work. The contribution is primarily the application and empirical analysis, rather than a substantially new statistical method. The appendix comparisons do not establish a clear advantage in detection power or computational cost over existing tests.

The practical recommendations exceed the evidence. Table 2 offers only a small collection of tasks, including an intentionally label-aligned synthetic example, without a validated threshold or prospective evaluation of augmentation decisions. The task-dependent score depends on the canonicalizer and prediction model. Furthermore, Figure 6 recommends equivariant methods when distributional bias is absent, despite the paper's own interpolation-threshold example showing that augmentation can hurt in that setting.

The downstream evaluation has important limitations. Section D.4.1 explicitly reports minimum test MAE across training epochs, introducing test-set selection bias. The principal ModelNet40 comparison also uses relatively weak models and a custom 80/10/10 split. Although an additional transformer supports the qualitative finding, stronger task-appropriate baselines and validation-selected checkpoints are needed to establish its generality.

Classifier accuracy measures distinguishability rather than a uniquely calibrated degree of canonicalization. With continuous groups, distributions supported on one orientation or many discrete orientations can both attain perfect discrimination. Conversely, low accuracy can reflect limited classifier capacity or optimization. The paper acknowledges these limitations, but some interpretations of high scores as sparse preferred orientations and low local scores as greater isotropy remain stronger than the diagnostic alone supports.

The connection between theory and realistic networks remains limited: the central harmful-augmentation construction concerns Gaussian linear regression, near-zero regularization, and a specially structured covariance. Experiments do not establish whether the same mechanism persists with tuned regularization or explains the observed neural-network results.
